definition: In classical Islamic jurisprudence, a man with congenital gender inversion — naturally effeminate in voice, movement, and manner — legally distinguished from one who deliberately imitates women.
notes: The Prophet reportedly tolerated mukhannathun in women's spaces until one was found describing women's bodies to men; the category carries no inherent sin unlike the mutakhannith, making it a genuine third-gender legal status.

definition: A man who deliberately adopts feminine mannerisms, clothing, or speech; condemned in multiple hadith traditions and legally distinguished from the naturally effeminate mukhannath.
notes: The Arabic Form V verbal pattern (tafaʿʿala) encodes deliberate, volitional action, making the condemnation categorically moral; modern speakers often conflate this term with mukhannath, erasing the jurisprudentially significant natural/deliberate distinction.

definition: A woman who deliberately adopts masculine attributes, behavior, or appearance; the female counterpart to the mutakhannith in classical Islamic jurisprudence.
notes: Considerably rarer in classical sources than its male counterpart; cursed alongside men who imitate women in the same Sahih al-Bukhari hadith; the Form X verbal root implies actively seeking to appropriate maleness.

definition: A face covering or mask associated with mukhannathun in classical Arabic social and performative contexts, marking their liminal gender status and mediating their access to gender-segregated spaces.
notes: Attestations are sparse and the term is highly obscure; may also denote a disguise or covering used more broadly in gender-ambiguous performance; root ق-ن-ع shares a semantic field with concealment and satisfaction, suggesting the veil simultaneously hides and resolves gender ambiguity.

definition: A descriptive compound noun phrase meaning 'the feminine man' or 'the womanly man,' used in modern standard Arabic to characterize an effeminate male.
notes: More descriptive and less formally condemnatory than the classical jurisprudential terms; encountered in MSA journalism, literary criticism, and contemporary social commentary; connotation ranges from neutral description to implicit stigma depending on context.

definition: A man who deliberately imitates or resembles women in manner or dress; drawn almost verbatim from hadith texts in which such men are cursed alongside women who imitate men.
notes: The phrase is nearly verbatim from Sahih al-Bukhari (hadith 5885); in modern religious discourse it functions primarily as a condemnation formula invoked against gender-nonconforming men; maps only approximately to cross-dressing since the condemnation targets behavioral imitation broadly, not clothing specifically.

definition: A woman who deliberately imitates or resembles men in manner or dress; the female counterpart in the same hadith tradition that condemns gender-crossing behavior.
notes: Paired symmetrically with the male equivalent in Sahih al-Bukhari; applied in modern contexts to condemn masculine-presenting women, short hair, or trousers on women; carries less social intensity in practice than its male counterpart in most contemporary Arabic-speaking contexts.

definition: A classical Arabic literary and cultural tradition of deliberate moral transgression, encompassing bawdy poetry, wine celebration, explicit homoeroticism, and erotic verse, cultivated as an aesthetic and social stance by poets such as Abu Nuwas and al-Akhtal al-Saghir.
notes: Mujūn is simultaneously a literary genre, an ethical posture of deliberate irreverence, and a social performance; 'libertinism' is the closest English approximation but misses the specific aesthetic tradition and the playful provocation of religious norms as a compositional strategy.

definition: The classical Arabic tradition of amatory and love poetry, ranging from chaste Platonic longing (ʿudhrī ghazal) to explicitly erotic verse (ḥissī ghazal), constituting one of the major classical Arabic poetic genres.
notes: Ghazal spans a wide register from spiritualized longing to explicit eroticism; the mapping to erotica applies only to the ḥissī (sensual) subtype; the broader genre category includes non-erotic verse and is better characterized as amatory poetry.

definition: An ode or extended poem explicitly treating sexual intercourse, erotic technique, and carnal pleasure, using the archaic Arabic term 'bāh' as a genre marker for sexuality.
notes: 'Bāh' (باه) is a classical Arabic synonym for coitus, sexual capacity, and erotic pleasure, now largely archaic; major works bearing this title include encyclopedic sexual manuals framed as verse; the qaṣīdat al-bāh genre overlaps with the broader kutub al-bāh (books of sexuality) tradition.

definition: The corpus of classical Arabic bawdy and libertine literature, encompassing erotic poetry, risqué anecdotes, and transgressive prose cultivated as a high-culture aesthetic tradition from the Abbasid period onward.
notes: Adab al-mujūn is distinct from pornography in that it is a self-conscious high-culture literary tradition; major contributors include Abu Nuwas, al-Jahiz (in adjacent registers), and numerous Abbasid court poets; the term 'adab' signals literary cultivation, making this learned transgression rather than crude obscenity.

definition: The amatory prelude that opens a classical Arabic qasida, in which the poet laments the departure of the beloved and describes her beauty — often in sensual or erotic terms — before transitioning to the ode's main panegyric or other themes.
notes: The nasīb is a structurally defined element of the classical Arabic ode with no English literary equivalent; its erotic content varies from mild longing to explicit sensuality; its presence is a formal expectation of the qasida genre such that its omission was itself a rhetorical statement.

definition: The classical Arabic genre of wine poetry, celebrating alcohol, beautiful cup-bearers, and sensual pleasure, frequently intertwined with homoerotic themes in the work of Abbasid poets such as Abu Nuwas.
notes: Khamriyyāt maps only loosely to erotica; it is a distinct genre in which erotic themes are frequent but not constitutive; 'Bacchic poetry' is used in English scholarship; the genre was theologically transgressive in an Islamic context, lending the eroticism an additional edge of religious provocation.

definition: A scholarly-constructed term for poetry treating sexual confinement, erotic repression, or the captivity of desire, extending the classical ḥabsiyyāt (prison poetry) genre into explicitly sexual territory.
notes: This appears to be a modern scholarly construction rather than an attested classical genre designation; the ḥabsiyyāt genre proper concerns physical imprisonment; appending al-jins creates a specialized critical term; recognition is extremely low and confined to academic discourse on classical Arabic poetics.

definition: A modern analytical term for erotic poetry, using the Greek-derived Arabic loanword 'ʾīrūsī' (from Eros) as a genre descriptor in literary criticism and comparative poetics.
notes: A descriptive scholarly label rather than a classical genre name; the loanword 'ʾīrūsī' signals a modern or Western-influenced academic framing; used to discuss both classical Arabic erotic traditions and translated Western erotic literature in Arabic-language literary studies.

definition: A theological and literary phrase meaning 'the sinful body' or 'the erring body,' encoding the concept that the physical self is inherently prone to moral transgression, particularly sexual sin.
notes: A phrasal construction rather than a fixed lexeme; encountered in Islamic philosophical, Sufi, and ascetic discourse about the nafs (self) and its bodily desires; 'khāṭiʾ' (erring, sinful) implies the body actively errs rather than passively tempting, distinguishing it slightly from concupiscence's theological framing of inherited desire.

definition: A theological and literary phrase meaning 'the shame of the body' or 'bodily disgrace,' encoding the concept that the body and its desires are inherently shameful and spiritually dangerous.
notes: 'Khizī' denotes disgrace and humiliation rather than merely embarrassment; used in Islamic ascetic and Sufi discourse about the spiritual dangers of bodily appetite; the phrase constructs shame as ontologically attached to the body rather than as a response to specific acts.

definition: A theological and literary phrase meaning 'the curse of desire' or 'the curse of lust,' framing sexual appetite as a divine punishment or a condemned affliction of the soul.
notes: 'Shahwa' (شهوة) is the standard Quranic word for desire/lust and carries significant theological weight; 'laʿna' (divine curse) adds formal condemnation; the phrase frames lust not merely as a temptation but as a punishment visited upon humanity, paralleling certain Christian readings of concupiscence as a consequence of the Fall.

definition: A Quranic term denoting ritual and moral impurity, filth, or abomination; applied to prohibited substances, acts, and behaviors including sexual transgressions of the gravest kind.
notes: Appears multiple times in the Quran (e.g., 5:90 on wine and gambling as rijs; 9:125 on hypocrites); 'indecency' substantially understates the term's gravity — rijs designates the most severe category of moral contamination and is closer to 'abomination' in weight; its Quranic authority gives it unique rhetorical force in religious condemnation of sexual transgression.

definition: Moral or ritual defilement, pollution, or contamination; describes the spiritual stain left by sexual transgression or contact with morally impure acts and people.
notes: Danas occupies the semantic space between ritual impurity (najāsa, addressed by wuḍūʾ) and moral contamination; in sexual discourse it implies the polluting effect of illicit acts on a person's spiritual standing; also used metaphorically for any corrupting moral influence.

definition: Filthiness, dirtiness, or moral squalor; used in sexual contexts to characterize obscene acts, language, or people as viscerally repugnant and degrading.
notes: Used for both physical uncleanliness and moral depravity; in sexual registers it emphasizes visceral disgust rather than formal jurisprudential impurity; the abstract noun form makes it slightly more literary than the adjective qadhir, though both are common across registers.

definition: Dirty, filthy, or morally repugnant; an adjective applied both to physically unclean things and to sexually obscene acts, speech, or people.
notes: One of the most common and universally recognized Arabic words for moral-sexual disgust; simultaneously physical and moral in connotation; applied freely to obscene speech, pornographic content, or sexually transgressive people; carries no technical register, making it the default crude condemnation across dialects.

definition: Obscene, indecent, or grossly lewd; a Quranic adjective and noun (fāḥisha, فاحشة) denoting grave moral transgression, particularly sexual indecency, fornication, or any act crossing the bounds of propriety.
notes: The root ف-ح-ش appears repeatedly in the Quran to condemn sexual misconduct; 'fāḥisha' (the noun) is the standard Quranic term for fornication and indecency (e.g., 4:15, 7:80); fāḥish carries this full jurisprudential and scriptural weight, making it substantially more grave than 'obscene' in English suggests.

definition: Vulgar, raucous, or sexually suggestive singing, speech, or behavior; especially associated in classical and colloquial usage with women's lewd, noisy, or sexually brazen conduct.
notes: Radaḥ carries gendered connotations, historically framing loud or sexually suggestive female behavior as socially transgressive; the concept overlaps with but is not equivalent to bawdy humor — it implies performative lewdness and social impropriety as much as sexual humor; also used in some modern dialects for noisy, vulgar arguing.

definition: Obscene, vulgar, foul-mouthed, or crudely indecent; applied to people, speech, or behavior that transgresses standards of sexual and social decency.
notes: Common across all Arabic-speaking regions and registers; frequently used to characterize sexually explicit or crude speech (kalām badhīʾ) and sexually transgressive people; in some contexts slightly stronger in condemnatory force than qadhir, emphasizing moral character over sensory disgust.
